claims.text: At elevated temperatures, FeNiCrCoCu thin-film wear resistance is primarily governed by formation of a stable, continuous oxide tribofilm.
The oxide tribofilm reduces direct contact between the coating and counterface.
Reduced direct metal contact decreases wear of the FeNiCrCoCu coating.
The proposed initial state is a uniformly deposited, as-deposited FeNiCrCoCu thin film on a conventional metal substrate without engineered oxide pretreatment.
Exposure to air before and during high-temperature wear testing is expected to increase surface oxidation relative to an inert-atmosphere baseline.
The relevant structural mediator is the presence and continuity of the surface oxide microstructure.
The protective surface layer may comprise mixed oxides of Fe, Ni, Cr, Co, and Cu.
Elevated temperature promotes oxidation of the FeNiCrCoCu coating's surface constituents.
Controlled oxidation produces a coherent oxide layer.
The coherent oxide layer acts as a sacrificial, low-shear interface.
A sacrificial, low-shear oxide interface reduces friction and wear.
Air-tested coatings should have a significantly lower wear rate than inert-atmosphere controls.
Air-tested coatings should exhibit a smoother worn surface than inert-atmosphere controls.
A uniform surface oxide layer should correlate with improved wear resistance.
The proposed mechanism is applicable approximately from 400°C to 600°C under consistent mechanical loading.
Temperatures or loads outside the proposed boundary may activate other failure mechanisms.
